nameStory: The Whitecross Jelly gets its name from the distinctive white cross pattern that decorates its transparent bell, making it look like a tiny floating religious symbol. This cross-shaped marking is so prominent that it's visible even when the jellyfish is swimming, giving it an almost mystical appearance in the water.
description: The Whitecross Jelly is a small, translucent jellyfish that drifts through cold coastal waters with an ethereal, glass-like appearance. Its most striking feature is the bright white cross pattern that stands out against its clear, dome-shaped bell. This delicate marine creature pulses gently through the water using rhythmic contractions of its bell. Like other jellyfish, it's made up mostly of water and has a soft, gelatinous body with trailing tentacles.

idTips.label: White Cross Pattern
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive bright white cross marking on the clear bell - it's sharp and well-defined, almost like it was painted on the transparent jelly

idTips.label: Clear Bell Shape
idTips.description: The bell is completely transparent like glass, with a smooth, dome-shaped appearance that you can see right through

idTips.label: Small Size
idTips.description: This is a relatively small jellyfish that fits easily in your field of view when spotted underwater

idTips.label: Trailing Tentacles
idTips.description: Fine, thread-like tentacles hang beneath the bell, often appearing as delicate streamers in the water

idTips.label: Pulsing Movement
idTips.description: Moves with gentle, rhythmic contractions of the bell, creating a graceful pumping motion through the water

habitat: Whitecross Jellies are found in the cold, shallow waters along New England's rocky coastlines and protected bays. They prefer cooler temperatures and are most commonly spotted near the surface in areas with good water circulation. Look for them in tide pools, shallow coves, and near rocky outcroppings where cold currents flow.

seasonality.spring: This is prime time for spotting Whitecross Jellies as water temperatures are ideal and they become more active in shallow areas.
seasonality.summer: Still present but may move to deeper or shadier waters to escape warming temperatures, making them harder to spot from shore.
seasonality.fall: Often return to shallower waters as temperatures cool, providing good viewing opportunities before winter sets in.
seasonality.winter: Present but less visible due to rough seas and their tendency to stay in deeper waters during the coldest months.

funFact: Despite being made of 95% water and having no brain, heart, or blood, the Whitecross Jelly can navigate ocean currents and hunt for prey with remarkable precision - it's essentially a living, breathing water balloon that's been perfecting its design for over 500 million years!
confusionNotes: The white cross pattern is so distinctive that it's rarely confused with other jellyfish species - if you see that bright white cross on a clear bell, you've found your Whitecross Jelly! Other clear jellies in New England waters lack this specific cross marking.
contextualKnowledge: This species is extremely rare in New England waters, with only one documented observation in the region, making any sighting particularly special and worth reporting to local marine biology organizations.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus documented in New England, the Whitecross Jelly stands apart from other regional jellies primarily due to its signature white cross pattern. While other jellyfish in the same family (Laodiceidae) may have clear bells, none display this distinctive cross marking, making identification relatively straightforward once you spot one.
